meta.title: Chiesi Data Bootcamp — Business Agility → Stakeholders → Problem Space → Data & AI Flexibility → Hackathon → Action → Cases
meta.subtitle: A simple knowledge lattice for a data bootcamp where people from finance, BI, marketing, strategy, sales and product development learn to use data and AI with greater agility in real business challenges.
meta.domainName: Professional learning, business agility, data and AI use in Chiesi
meta.searchPlaceholder: agility, business-as-usual, finance, BI, marketing, strategy, sales, product development, data confidence, AI prompting, hackathon, stakeholder needs, interprofessional learning, Similar Deals, Green Analysis, Pipeline Next…
meta.userContextPlaceholder: e.g., finance needs clearer value assumptions; BI wants trusted data definitions; marketing needs market insight; students are helping explore problem spaces; hackathon team is working on Green Analysis…
meta.promptTemplate:
You are helping Chiesi participants develop agility in the face of technical and business challenges.

Use the selected concepts to write a practical learning narrative about how a mixed hackathon team moves from a business-as-usual concern to a clearer problem, a small data/AI experiment, and a decision-ready output.

User context (if provided):
{{USER_CONTEXT}}

Selected concepts:
{{SELECTED_TITLES}}

Details:
{{SELECTED_DETAILS}}

Trace paths:
{{TRACE_SUMMARY}}

Deliver:
- The business setting and stakeholder concerns
- The problem-space questions the team asks
- How students and business participants work together
- How data and AI are used flexibly, without overclaiming
- What the hackathon prototype shows
- What caveats, human review points and limits are made visible
- How the work builds agility: better questions, more options, clearer action and stronger cross-team collaboration
- One practical next step for business-as-usual adoption

levels.title: Business agility and purpose
levels.hint: The broad aim: people become more able to act with data, AI and judgement in real business situations.

levels.title: Everyday business concerns
levels.hint: The normal pressures people bring from finance, BI, marketing, strategy, sales, product development, sustainability and leadership.

levels.title: Problem-space exploration
levels.hint: How mixed groups turn a broad concern into a clear decision, user need, data question and learning path.

levels.title: Flexible data and AI use
levels.hint: Simple capability: handle data confidently, ask better questions, use AI well, and know where human judgement is needed.

levels.title: Hackathon ways of working
levels.hint: The bootcamp in action: students and business participants explore, test, build, explain and learn together.

levels.title: Decision outputs and new habits
levels.hint: What the work produces: clearer evidence packs, better meetings, shared language, reusable workflows and changed practice.

levels.title: Cases and watch-outs
levels.hint: Concrete examples from Similar Deals, Green Analysis and Pipeline Next, plus common risks to avoid.

nodes.label: Agility to act
nodes.summary: The ability to move from a business issue to useful action with data, AI and people.
nodes.bodyHtml: Agility means being able to shift between the big picture and the practical next step: the decision, the data, the people, the tool, the caveat and the action.

nodes.label: Seeing more options
nodes.summary: Technical confidence expands what people think the business can try.
nodes.bodyHtml: As participants understand data and AI, they see more routes through a problem: a quick check, a better question, a prototype, a reusable workflow, or a new cross-team conversation.

nodes.label: Shared business purpose
nodes.summary: Data work should serve Chiesi’s real business aims, not become a side activity.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp connects learning to business value: better decisions, less waste, more joined-up work, and more useful use of internal and external data.

nodes.label: Whole-business view
nodes.summary: Participants learn to see how one team’s data affects another team’s decision.
nodes.bodyHtml: A deal, emission trend or pipeline review is not owned by one function alone. It crosses finance, BI, marketing, sales, strategy, product and operational teams.

nodes.label: Human judgement with AI
nodes.summary: AI supports judgement; it should not replace responsibility.
nodes.bodyHtml: The goal is not automatic answers. It is better use of evidence, clearer caveats, and stronger human decisions.

nodes.label: Confidence with limits
nodes.summary: Good data work increases confidence while keeping limits visible.
nodes.bodyHtml: Participants learn to be confident without overclaiming: to show what is known, what is uncertain, and what still needs expert review.

nodes.label: Business-as-usual pressure
nodes.summary: People join the bootcamp while still carrying normal workload, deadlines and stakeholder needs.
nodes.bodyHtml: The learning journey must respect everyday pressure. It should help people improve work they already care about, not add abstract tasks.

nodes.label: Finance: value and control
nodes.summary: Finance cares about value, cost, risk, forecasts, assumptions and decision confidence.
nodes.bodyHtml: Finance participants may ask whether a data or AI output can support a business case, explain assumptions, reduce rework, or make value clearer.

nodes.label: BI: reliable reporting
nodes.summary: Business intelligence cares about trusted data, clear definitions and repeatable reporting.
nodes.bodyHtml: BI participants often bring a concern for consistency: one version of the story, clear data sources, and outputs that can be repeated without manual repair.

nodes.label: Marketing: customer and market signal
nodes.summary: Marketing cares about insight, positioning, market change and customer understanding.
nodes.bodyHtml: Marketing participants may ask how external evidence, internal data and AI summaries can help explain what matters to customers and markets.

nodes.label: Strategy: choices and fit
nodes.summary: Strategy cares about options, trade-offs, timing and fit with wider company direction.
nodes.bodyHtml: Strategy participants may ask whether data can reveal better options, compare pathways and make assumptions visible before decisions are locked in.

nodes.label: Sales: field reality
nodes.summary: Sales cares about what happens with customers, regions, channels and practical adoption.
nodes.bodyHtml: Sales participants can test whether an output is useful in the real world: understandable, timely, trusted, and connected to customer-facing action.

nodes.label: Product development: pipeline fit
nodes.summary: Product development cares about assets, evidence, stages, risks and next milestones.
nodes.bodyHtml: Product and pipeline colleagues help link metrics, narratives and expert judgement so that reviews focus on decisions rather than data repair.

nodes.label: Sustainability: action and proof
nodes.summary: Sustainability cares about emissions, drivers, targets, action plans and credible evidence.
nodes.bodyHtml: Sustainability colleagues need analysis that connects numbers to levers, owners and uncertainty rather than only showing totals.

nodes.label: Leadership: decision need
nodes.summary: Leaders need concise evidence that helps them decide what to do next.
nodes.bodyHtml: Executive users usually need a clear story: what changed, why it matters, what is uncertain, and what action is recommended.

nodes.label: Stakeholder trust
nodes.summary: Outputs must be trusted by people with different roles and concerns.
nodes.bodyHtml: Trust grows when outputs are transparent, caveated, useful and connected to existing meetings and responsibilities.

nodes.label: Beyond time saved
nodes.summary: The value is not only speed; it is better shared understanding and better action.
nodes.bodyHtml: Saving time matters, but the deeper value is reducing confusion, improving evidence, and helping departments act together.

nodes.label: Problem space first
nodes.summary: Start with the business problem before choosing a tool.
nodes.bodyHtml: The first move is to understand the decision, the users, the current friction and the evidence needed. Only then should the team discuss technology.

nodes.label: Decision-backwards thinking
nodes.summary: Begin with the decision that should be better after the work.
nodes.bodyHtml: A team asks: which meeting, choice or conversation should improve, and what evidence would make that possible?

nodes.label: Stakeholder map
nodes.summary: Name the people affected by the problem and the output.
nodes.bodyHtml: The map includes users, sponsors, data owners, decision-makers, technical helpers and people who may challenge the output.

nodes.label: Current workflow map
nodes.summary: Show how work is done now, including delays and workarounds.
nodes.bodyHtml: Mapping current work reveals where information is lost, where people repeat tasks, and where a small change could help.

nodes.label: Pain point to question
nodes.summary: Turn frustration into a clear question that can be tested.
nodes.bodyHtml: For example, 'the review is slow' becomes 'which conflicting asset fields should be flagged before the meeting?'

nodes.label: User story
nodes.summary: Describe the need from the viewpoint of a real user.
nodes.bodyHtml: A user story keeps the work grounded: 'As a strategy lead, I need to see why these deals are comparable so I can judge the opportunity.'

nodes.label: Shared business terms
nodes.summary: Agree simple meanings for terms such as similar, forecast, flag, driver and confidence.
nodes.bodyHtml: Teams often use the same word differently. Shared terms make links up and down the lattice clearer.

nodes.label: Visible assumptions
nodes.summary: Make hidden assumptions explicit before building.
nodes.bodyHtml: Assumptions may concern deal similarity, emissions drivers, pipeline status, data quality or what a user will accept as credible.

nodes.label: Boundaries of use
nodes.summary: Say what the output is for and what it must not be used for.
nodes.bodyHtml: A prototype may support discussion, exploration and learning. It should not be treated as a final automated decision.

nodes.label: Success signal
nodes.summary: Define what would make the experiment useful.
nodes.bodyHtml: A success signal might be a better discussion, a clearer caveat, a reusable data slice, or a sponsor saying the output would change a meeting.

nodes.label: Questions become artefacts
nodes.summary: Every good question should produce something concrete.
nodes.bodyHtml: Questions can produce a source list, workflow map, field list, assumption table, prompt, mock-up, test rule or demo plan.

nodes.label: Students as problem explorers
nodes.summary: Students help open the problem space rather than simply receive instructions.
nodes.bodyHtml: Students can ask fresh questions, map unclear areas, test first ideas and help business participants see the challenge from new angles.

nodes.label: Interprofessional learning
nodes.summary: People from different roles learn by making sense of the same challenge together.
nodes.bodyHtml: Finance, BI, marketing, strategy, sales and product colleagues each see different parts of the problem. Learning happens when these views are brought into one shared task.

nodes.label: Flexible data handling
nodes.summary: Being able to work with data in different forms without needing to be a specialist.
nodes.bodyHtml: Participants do not need to master every tool. They need enough confidence to inspect, question, clean, combine and explain data with help.

nodes.label: Data source awareness
nodes.summary: Know where useful data may come from, inside and outside the organisation.
nodes.bodyHtml: A useful answer may combine internal files, external market information, expert notes, business narratives and safe simulated datasets.

nodes.label: Data quality awareness
nodes.summary: Notice missing, old, inconsistent, vague or misleading data.
nodes.bodyHtml: Quality awareness helps people ask: can we trust this field, what changed, who owns it, and what caveat should be shown?

nodes.label: Joining data awareness
nodes.summary: Understand why connecting records is powerful and risky.
nodes.bodyHtml: People learn that linking sources can create new insight, but only if identifiers, definitions and timing are handled carefully.

nodes.label: Small safe data slice
nodes.summary: Use a limited, safe dataset that is enough to test the idea.
nodes.bodyHtml: A hackathon does not need every system. It needs a small slice that proves whether the logic is useful.

nodes.label: Data story
nodes.summary: Explain what the data suggests in plain business language.
nodes.bodyHtml: The point is not just a chart. It is a clear account of what changed, what matters and what action might follow.

nodes.label: AI prompting for agility
nodes.summary: Use AI to ask better questions, explore options and draft useful outputs.
nodes.bodyHtml: Prompting is not just asking for answers. It is a way to test ideas, compare options, create drafts, expose assumptions and speed up learning.

nodes.label: AI as work partner
nodes.summary: AI can support thinking, summarising, comparing and drafting, while people stay responsible.
nodes.bodyHtml: AI becomes useful when it is linked to a clear task, good evidence, review steps and human judgement.

nodes.label: AI limits
nodes.summary: AI can sound confident while being wrong, incomplete or unclear about sources.
nodes.bodyHtml: Participants learn to check outputs, ask for evidence, spot overclaiming and avoid treating AI as authority.

nodes.label: Prompt to decision
nodes.summary: Shape prompts around the business decision and needed caveats.
nodes.bodyHtml: A strong prompt says who the output is for, what decision it supports, what evidence to use, and what uncertainty to show.

nodes.label: Plain explanation
nodes.summary: Explain data and AI outputs without technical fog.
nodes.bodyHtml: Plain explanation lets mixed teams challenge, improve and trust the work.

nodes.label: Light tool awareness
nodes.summary: Know what tools can broadly do without needing deep detail.
nodes.bodyHtml: Participants gain awareness of spreadsheets, simple scripts, AI assistants, visual tools and workflow tools, but the focus remains on business use.

nodes.label: Human review points
nodes.summary: Decide where people must inspect, approve or challenge an output.
nodes.bodyHtml: Good use of AI and data places human judgement at important points: caveats, exceptions, high-risk claims and final decisions.

nodes.label: Hackathon as learning lab
nodes.summary: The hackathon is a safe place to explore, build, test and learn quickly.
nodes.bodyHtml: It is not about a finished product. It is about finding a credible pathway from business need to useful data-enabled action.

nodes.label: Mixed-team exploration
nodes.summary: Business participants, students and mentors work together across roles.
nodes.bodyHtml: Different perspectives help the team see the problem more fully and avoid building something that only one function understands.

nodes.label: Student-business partnership
nodes.summary: Students bring energy, questions and technical curiosity; business participants bring context and judgement.
nodes.bodyHtml: The partnership works when neither side dominates: students explore and prototype, while business stakeholders guide what matters.

nodes.label: Rapid mock-up
nodes.summary: Create a quick, visible version of the idea.
nodes.bodyHtml: A mock-up can be a sketch, table, simple prompt, sample output or clickable demo. It helps people discuss the idea sooner.

nodes.label: Build-test-learn loop
nodes.summary: Try a small step, show it, learn from it, and improve it.
nodes.bodyHtml: This loop makes agility visible. The team learns by moving between concept, data, AI output, feedback and next action.

nodes.label: Safe to try
nodes.summary: Use prototypes to learn without risking live business decisions.
nodes.bodyHtml: Safe experiments let teams test assumptions, discover limits and build confidence before adoption.

nodes.label: Clear team roles
nodes.summary: Give people simple roles such as challenge owner, data finder, prompt tester, explainer and reviewer.
nodes.bodyHtml: Clear roles keep work moving and make space for different strengths.

nodes.label: Mentor support
nodes.summary: Mentors help teams move when they get stuck.
nodes.bodyHtml: Mentors can translate between business questions and technical possibilities, without taking ownership away from the team.

nodes.label: Challenge-owner check-in
nodes.summary: Regularly ask the business owner whether the work still matters.
nodes.bodyHtml: Check-ins stop teams drifting into interesting but irrelevant outputs.

nodes.label: Show and tell
nodes.summary: Teams explain what they tried, what worked, what failed and what they learned.
nodes.bodyHtml: Show and tell turns prototype work into shared learning for the wider group.

nodes.label: Peer teaching
nodes.summary: Participants teach one another small useful moves.
nodes.bodyHtml: Peer teaching may involve explaining a dataset, a prompt, a chart, a caveat or a business concern in simple language.

nodes.label: Problem-space gallery
nodes.summary: Display each team’s problem map, assumptions and early outputs.
nodes.bodyHtml: A shared gallery helps teams compare challenges and see links between cases.

nodes.label: Demo with caveats
nodes.summary: Show the prototype and also show what it cannot yet do.
nodes.bodyHtml: A mature demo says: here is the promise, here is the evidence, here are the limits, and here is the next test.

nodes.label: Decision pack
nodes.summary: A clear evidence pack for a real meeting or decision.
nodes.bodyHtml: The pack should show key evidence, assumptions, caveats, options and next actions in a way decision-makers can use.

nodes.label: Better meeting
nodes.summary: A meeting spends less time fixing data and more time deciding what to do.
nodes.bodyHtml: The strongest sign of value may be a better conversation: clearer evidence, less confusion and faster agreement on next steps.

nodes.label: One-page story
nodes.summary: A concise explanation of the issue, evidence and decision need.
nodes.bodyHtml: A one-page story helps stakeholders from different roles see the same problem and challenge it constructively.

nodes.label: Reusable workflow
nodes.summary: A repeatable way of working, not a one-off hackathon result.
nodes.bodyHtml: A useful prototype points towards a process that can be repeated with new data, new cases or new decisions.

nodes.label: Shared language
nodes.summary: Teams develop common words for data, AI, uncertainty and action.
nodes.bodyHtml: Shared language helps Chiesi link business concerns, data issues and technical options across departments.

nodes.label: Joined-up action
nodes.summary: Different teams can coordinate around a clearer evidence base.
nodes.bodyHtml: The aim is not just insight; it is action that connects departments and reduces fragmented work.

nodes.label: Adoption path
nodes.summary: Agree what would be needed to move from prototype to normal work.
nodes.bodyHtml: The path may include data access, owner approval, review steps, training, system fit and business sponsorship.

nodes.label: Light governance
nodes.summary: Use enough control to protect trust without stopping learning.
nodes.bodyHtml: For early prototypes, governance can be simple: clear scope, safe data, human review, caveats and next-step ownership.

nodes.label: Learning loop
nodes.summary: Capture what the team learned and feed it back into the next build.
nodes.bodyHtml: Learning loops help the organisation remember: which data worked, which assumptions failed, and which questions got sharper.

nodes.label: Business value test
nodes.summary: Ask whether the output would improve a real business decision.
nodes.bodyHtml: The test is practical: would someone use this, trust this, challenge this and act differently because of it?

nodes.label: Better questions
nodes.summary: Participants leave able to ask sharper business and data questions.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp succeeds when people can frame better questions even before a tool is selected.

nodes.label: New work habits
nodes.summary: People start using data and AI more thoughtfully in normal work.
nodes.bodyHtml: New habits include checking assumptions, asking for sources, using AI for drafts, naming caveats, and involving other roles early.

nodes.label: Confidence to collaborate
nodes.summary: Participants become more comfortable working across functions on data-rich problems.
nodes.bodyHtml: Confidence grows because people have practised asking questions, making artefacts, testing ideas and explaining uncertainty together.

nodes.label: Case: Similar Deals
nodes.summary: Find comparable deals for a business decision, with reasons and caveats.
nodes.bodyHtml: The challenge is not to produce a long deal list. It is to make comparison useful, explainable and relevant to the decision.

nodes.label: Case: Green Analysis
nodes.summary: Turn emissions history into useful forecasts, scenarios and action evidence.
nodes.bodyHtml: The challenge is to connect emissions, business drivers, assumptions and possible interventions without hiding uncertainty.

nodes.label: Case: Pipeline Next
nodes.summary: Bring asset metrics and narratives into a clearer review process.
nodes.bodyHtml: The challenge is to combine data and narrative so review meetings focus on decisions rather than data repair.

nodes.label: Watch-out: false friend deals
nodes.summary: Two deals can look similar but matter for very different reasons.
nodes.bodyHtml: A therapy-area match may hide differences in stage, deal type, strategic aim, geography or financial structure.

nodes.label: Watch-out: same emissions, different story
nodes.summary: The same emissions number can have several business meanings.
nodes.bodyHtml: A change may reflect production volume, supplier changes, emission factors, boundary changes, travel rebound or real operational progress.

nodes.label: Watch-out: pipeline data conflict
nodes.summary: A metric, slide and risk note may tell different stories.
nodes.bodyHtml: The useful output is not a polished summary. It is a flag that shows where expert review is needed.

nodes.label: Watch-out: tool first
nodes.summary: Choosing a tool before the problem is clear leads to weak results.
nodes.bodyHtml: The team may build something impressive but irrelevant if it has not named the decision, user and evidence need.

nodes.label: Watch-out: too much detail
nodes.summary: Technical detail can overwhelm stakeholders and hide the business point.
nodes.bodyHtml: The right level of detail depends on the audience. Most stakeholders need enough to trust and challenge, not every method step.

nodes.label: Watch-out: AI sounds right
nodes.summary: AI can produce fluent outputs that still need checking.
nodes.bodyHtml: Participants should ask for sources, caveats and review points, especially when outputs will influence decisions.

nodes.label: Watch-out: data silo
nodes.summary: A team may optimise its own data while missing the wider business link.
nodes.bodyHtml: The bootcamp should help teams see where data crosses departmental boundaries.

nodes.label: Watch-out: scope too big
nodes.summary: Trying to solve everything at once weakens the hackathon.
nodes.bodyHtml: A smaller slice with a clear decision is more useful than a large, vague ambition.

nodes.label: Success pattern: small, clear, useful
nodes.summary: A strong hackathon result is small enough to test and clear enough to use.
nodes.bodyHtml: Good teams show a real problem, a safe data slice, a simple output, clear caveats, sponsor feedback and a next step.
